article_content: Greece has appointed a senior judge as the country's new caretaker prime minister after political parties failed to form a coalition government. Panagiotis Pikrammenos, head of the Council of State, was sworn in on Wednesday. The 67-year-old will oversee the organization of repeat elections on June 17, which analysts predict will likely result in a hung parliament. This could lead to further political instability and potential chaos in the eurozone. A radical left coalition, led by Alexis Tsipras, has gained significant support and could push Greece towards a collision course with the European Union. EU leaders have stated that Greece will not receive any further loans unless it adheres to strict debt-reducing measures. The situation has caused widespread panic in European markets, threatening to destabilize the entire eurozone. In their first official talks, French President Francois Hollande and German Chancellor Angela Merkel emphasized their support for Greece remaining in the currency union, but warned that the country must honor its austerity commitments. 'We want Greece to stay in the eurozone, but the agreements made by the previous government must be upheld. The Greek people must decide their future in the euro area,' Merkel said. EU Commission President Jose Manuel Barroso echoed this sentiment, stating that while the EU wants Greece to remain, there is no alternative to the austerity plan. Greek voters will have to decide whether to stay in the eurozone, amid growing fears of a catastrophic exit. The political deadlock has raised concerns among eurozone ministers that Greece will fail to meet its austerity commitments, leading to potential chaos. Massive protests have erupted across Greece, with violent clashes reported in multiple cities. Some information for this report was provided by AP and AFP.

article_content: Sudanese human rights activists are sounding the alarm, urging the international community to brace for an impending disaster. Critical aid supplies are dwindling rapidly, and President Omar Al-Bashir's expulsion of 13 NGOs has plunged Darfur into chaos. Without immediate intervention, millions will be forced to flee in search of survival. Activists in Geneva are pleading with the UN Human Rights Council and aid agencies to intervene as the situation spirals out of control. The expulsions have cut off 50% of the aid reaching displaced persons, leaving them on the brink of starvation. Following his ICC indictment, President Al-Bashir's actions have put millions at risk. Mahmoud Braima of the Darfur Association warns that 2.7 million are immediately affected, with 4.7 million more facing indirect consequences. Food and water shortages are imminent, and disease outbreaks loom as the rainy season approaches. Braima fears a mass exodus to countries like Chad and the Central African Republic, overwhelming already strained resources. The Sudanese government has shown no capacity to fill the aid gap, and activists allege a deliberate effort to starve and sicken the population. The international community must act now to prevent what many are calling a 'humanitarian crisis.' Pre-positioning aid in neighboring countries is the only hope to mitigate this escalating disaster.

article_content: Former airline boss Christopher Luxon formally took office as New Zealand's prime minister Monday, vowing to drastically cut inflation and immediately lower interest rates. Luxon took over six weeks after his conservative National Party won national elections, ending a six-year Labour Party reign ushered in by Jacinda Ardern. Luxon, 53, once chief executive of Air New Zealand, was sworn in as head of a new coalition government by New Zealand's governor-general in a ceremony in the capital Wellington. 'It is an honour and an awesome responsibility,' Luxon told reporters. 'The number one job is to fix the economy. We have to reduce the cost of living and get inflation under control so we can lower interest rates and make food more affordable.' Luxon said his new government would also focus in its first few months on restoring law and order and improving public services. 'We need to go to work,' he said. The former Labour government had struggled to control the rising cost of living, a global issue blamed in part on pandemic-related supply issues and Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The previous prime minister, Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins, took over from Ardern in January. She had unexpectedly resigned, calling an end to her five-year period in office because she no longer had 'enough in the tank.' Luxon said his cabinet would meet over the next two days with a focus on signing off their plans for the first 100 days in office. National has promised to crack down on crime, ban cellphones in schools and scrap planned fuel tax hikes. 'A lot of our focus is on tackling the underlying cause of inflation,' Luxon said. 'That means a series of things to make sure we generate savings out of the public service and that government spending is prudent.' Luxon becomes the 42nd prime minister of New Zealand after protracted coalition talks came to an agreement on Friday. His National party has formed a three-party coalition with the conservative ACT and populist New Zealand First parties to govern in the 123-seat parliament. In a first for New Zealand, the deputy prime minister role will be shared in two 18-month stints. New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, 78, was sworn in alongside Luxon as deputy prime minister, but will hand over the role at the end of May 2025. He will be replaced by ACT leader David Seymour for the remainder of the three-year parliamentary term. Luxon, a father of two, is a wealthy teetotaller and lover of country music who rose to prominence when he ran the national airline for seven years before entering politics.
